For the NYISO’s AC Transmission Needs projects, the NYPSC identified an alternative cost allocation method that assigns more cost responsibility to the zones that receive economic benefits from the project. If an alternative is not used, project costs are applied across the entire region based on load ratio share in line with the view that policy-driven projects benefit all network users. The JTIQ projects present a different approach to backstop cost allocation. In this case, the projects are driven by interconnecting customers across multiple states and transmission planning regions rather than the policy of a single state. The costs to interconnecting customers are spread across multiple queue clusters to avoid prohibitively expensive costs for the first generators and free ridership for generators that connect later. To reduce the risk to project developers, electricity load in SPP and MISO serves as the backstop in case the transmission capacity is undersubscribed by generators. This approach enables the projects to move forward through the planning and permitting processes without the need to wait for generators to fully subscribe to the transmission capacity. 24 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 4 Cost Allocation Changes: Regulatory Paths Forward The previous sections outline existing methods and lessons learned for transmission cost allocation. This section presents the regulatory options for regions to update their cost allocation methods and compares the processes different regions have adopted to implement these options. 4.1 Regulatory Options To Update Cost Allocation Methods Implementing new or alternative cost allocation methods requires navigating formal procedures to revise RTO/ISO governing documents and/or transmission owner tariffs.12 These documents are institution-specific rules and operating procedures, and changes must be reviewed and approved by FERC. The three pathways to submit proposed amendments to these governing documents for FERC review are (1) compliance with FERC rulemaking, (2) exercising Federal Power Act (FPA) Section 206 filing rights, and (3) exercising FPA Section 205 filing rights. Compliance With Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Rulemaking FERC can require RTO/ISOs to revise their governing documents through a broad-based regulatory order. In general, FERC issues regulatory requirements or principles in the rulemaking order that allow for regional flexibility in each RTO/ISO’s compliance plan. To date, FERC rulemaking related to cost allocation has been limited. Order 1000 required regions to include a cost allocation method for new facilities selected through regional planning according to six principles (FERC 2011). Order 1920 builds on this but adds more structural and procedural guidelines related to developing a default or ex ante cost allocation method, state involvement, and engagement periods (Building for the Future Through Electric Regional Transmission Planning and Cost Allocation 2024). Exercising Federal Power Act Section 206 Filing Rights Section 206 filing rights are broadly available to different stakeholder groups, giving them the right to challenge existing RTO/ISO governance document provisions and give FERC the authority to investigate and modify these rates if they are found to be unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential (“Federal Power Act” 2018).
